title: Obedience (ch. 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tools of good works: a long list that ends on God's mercy. Your line was never despair.

A teenager is asked to take the trash out. He says sure. He even does it. But all the way down the driveway a speech runs in his head: why is it always me, nobody else ever does this, I was in the middle of something. The trash makes it to the curb. So does a small gray cloud. Saint Benedict gives that cloud a name: murmuring. In chapter five he goes after it, because in his Rule the task is only half the matter.
screen: `SURE, AND A SPEECH IN HIS HEAD.` → `THE TRASH GOES OUT. SO DOES A CLOUD.` → `BENEDICT CALLS IT MURMURING.`

segments.voice: Chapter five opens plainly: the first step of humility is obedience without delay. Benedict draws a picture. A monk is told to do something, and he puts down what's in his hands, unfinished, so that the hearing and the doing happen almost together. He ties this to words of Jesus in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that heareth you, heareth me." For Benedict, a word from the abbot is answered as though God were the one asking. Then he raises the bar. Doing the thing isn't enough. It should be done without hesitating, without dragging the feet, without coldness, without grumbling, and without a reply that shows unwillingness. He means the grumbling inside, too. If a monk obeys but murmurs in his heart, God sees the heart, and the work isn't accepted. For the other side he borrows a line from Paul: "God loveth a cheerful giver." The Rule keeps that high bar human in two ways. In a later chapter, a monk handed something that seems impossible may go to his superior, patiently and at a fitting moment, and explain why. Obedience isn't pretending a heavy load is light. And near the end of the Rule, Benedict says obedience is a good to be shown not only to the abbot but to one another. So it isn't a chain of command running downhill. It's a whole house leaning toward yes. Outside a monastery, nobody vows obedience to an abbot, but anyone can notice the speech that runs under a chore, and let it go quiet.
screen: `OBEDIENCE WITHOUT DELAY.` · `HE THAT HEARETH YOU, HEARETH ME.` · `NOT EVEN MURMURING IN THE HEART.` · `YOU MAY EXPLAIN. OBEY ONE ANOTHER.` · then, large: `GOD LOVETH A CHEERFUL GIVER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one task you'd rather skip today, the dishes, an email, a phone call, and picture starting it. Listen for the speech that starts up with it, the why me, the not now; don't argue, just let it get quieter on the out-breath, and picture your hands simply doing what hands do. If you pray, offer the task to God before you begin.
Obedience. For Benedict, a ready yes, given without delay and without grumbling, out loud or inside. Today's word.
Your line: no murmuring. The task is only half of it; the heart is the other half. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns promise obedience when they make their vows, and the community hears the Rule read aloud, including chapter five on obedience without delay or grumbling.

chat.says: If I do the chore but grumble the whole time, does it still count?
options: For Benedict, only half: he asks for a ready yes without murmuring, even inside.
Yes, for Benedict the job is all that counts; what you feel inside doesn't matter.
No, for Benedict a monk should refuse any task he can't do with a smile.
chat.meaning: Benedict says God sees the heart: a task done with inner murmuring isn't accepted. He quotes Paul: God loves a cheerful giver.

murmuring.meaning: Benedict's word for grumbling, out loud or inside

notes: The Rule is paraphrased throughout; no English translation of the Rule is on the public-domain list. Check: ch. 5 opens 'the first degree of humility is obedience without delay'; the monk leaves his work unfinished; the list 'not timidly, not tardily, not tepidly, not with murmuring, not with a reply showing unwillingness' is paraphrased as 'without hesitating, without dragging the feet, without coldness, without grumbling'; murmuring in the heart makes the work unacceptable to God.
Ch. 68 (impossible tasks: the monk may explain to his superior patiently and at a fitting time) and ch. 71 (obedience to one another) are summarized; confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Luke 10:16 and 2 Corinthians 9:7, both quoted in RB 5.
Pronunciation of 'oboedientia' given in Church Latin style; confirm.
